faq.a: It is the bedside clue that the kidney capsule is inflamed, prompting urgent evaluation for pyelonephritis or obstruction.
Yes, in systemic infections or bilateral obstruction, but unilateral pain is more typical of focal renal disease.
Rely on clinical assessment, plain X‑ray for stones, and early referral if obstruction or severe infection is suspected.
faq.q: What if ultrasound is not available?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with fever, dysuria and right‑sided CVA tenderness. What is your next step? — Obtain urine culture and start empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering resistant Gram‑negatives.
How does CVA tenderness help differentiate pyelonephritis from cystitis? — It indicates renal capsule involvement, which is absent in lower urinary tract infection.
A patient has CVA tenderness but normal creatinine and no fever. Which condition is most likely? — Early uncomplicated pyelonephritis or renal colic; assess for stones and consider analgesia.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in severe CVA tenderness with rising creatinine? — NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandin‑mediated perfusion, worsening renal injury.
In a resource‑limited setting, what is the minimum investigation to confirm pyelonephritis? — Urine dipstick for leukocyte esterase/nitrites plus microscopy; treat empirically if positive.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate referral for possible renal abscess? — Persistent fever >38.5 °C despite antibiotics plus a palpable flank mass.
How would you distinguish CVA tenderness due to pyelonephritis from musculoskeletal back pain? — Percussion elicits pain in pyelonephritis; movement of the spine worsens musculoskeletal pain.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with flank pain and CVA tenderness. What additional diagnosis should you consider? — Renal papillary necrosis; obtain ultrasound and manage pain and hydration.
ai.title: Costovertebral Angle Tenderness
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Costovertebral angle (CVA) tenderness signals inflammation of the renal capsule or parenchyma, most often pyelonephritis. Recognising it guides urgent investigation and treatment, especially where imaging is limited.

b: Positive when pain is reproduced by tapping the flank with the heel of the hand
Often bilateral in systemic disease, unilateral in focal renal pathology
sections.p: CVA tenderness is pain elicited by percussion over the angle between the 12th rib and the vertebral column. It reflects irritation of the renal capsule, usually from infection or obstruction.

b: Mild: fleeting discomfort, no fever
Moderate: pain with fever, urinary symptoms
Severe: pain with systemic toxicity, oliguria or rising creatinine
sections.p: Severity is judged clinically; there is no formal staging system. Persistent, severe pain suggests advanced infection or obstruction requiring urgent intervention.

b: Acute pyelonephritis – especially from E. coli, Proteus, or HIV‑related opportunists
Obstructive uropathy – stones, congenital pelvi‑ureteric junction obstruction, schistosomal fibrosis
Renal abscess or perinephric cellulitis – often secondary to untreated pyelonephritis
Tuberculous renal disease – chronic flank pain, weight loss
Trauma – blunt flank injury causing capsular bleed
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the commonest causes are infections and obstructive uropathy.

b: Unilateral pain radiating to the groin
Fever ≥38 °C, chills
Dysuria, urgency, or cloudy urine
Nausea or vomiting in severe infection
sections.p: Patients usually present with flank pain that worsens on percussion, fever, and urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency, or flank‑related urgency).

t.b: Detects leukocyte esterase and nitrites → suggests bacterial infection; negative does not rule out early pyelonephritis
Identifies causative organism and guides antibiotics; if culture unavailable, treat empirically based on local resistance patterns
Assesses renal function; rising creatinine signals obstruction or severe infection
Detects hydronephrosis, abscess, or large stones; if ultrasound unavailable, rely on clinical signs and plain X‑ray
Shows radiopaque stones; limited for soft tissue but useful where ultrasound is absent

b: Persistent fever >38.5 °C despite antibiotics
Oliguria or anuria
Rapid rise in serum creatinine
Hypotension or altered mental status
sections.p: Unrecognised or untreated CVA tenderness can progress to sepsis, renal abscess, or permanent loss of renal function.

b: Empiric oral/IV antibiotics covering Gram‑negative rods (e.g., ceftriaxone, gentamicin) – choose agents with renal safety and local susceptibility
Hydration to maintain urine flow
Analgesia with paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs if renal function is impaired
If obstruction suspected, arrange urgent decompression (ureteric stent or nephrostomy) – if not possible, refer to higher‑level centre
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration.

b: Repeat urine culture after treatment completion
Educate on early presentation for dysuria or flank pain
Screen for diabetes or HIV in recurrent cases
sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 48‑72 h; ensure symptom resolution and normalising labs. Prevent recurrence with hygiene, adequate fluid intake, and treating underlying urinary tract abnormalities.

b: Musculoskeletal back pain – pain worsens with movement, not percussion
Psoas sign from appendicitis – pain on hip extension, not flank percussion
Herpes zoster – dermatomal rash precedes pain
sections.p: Other sources of flank pain may mimic CVA tenderness.

b: Negative urine dipstick in early infection or when antibiotics already started
Normal creatinine in early obstruction; rely on imaging or persistent pain
sections.p: Certain investigations may be falsely reassuring.
